bib.title: SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text

question: Can a large, high-quality, span-based reading comprehension dataset on Wikipedia be built, and how hard is it for a feature-based baseline compared with humans?
contributions: SQuAD v1.0 dataset of 107,785 crowdsourced span-answer questions on 536 Wikipedia articles
Analysis of answer types, reasoning types and syntactic divergence via dependency-path edit distance
Logistic regression baseline (51.0 F1) and human performance measurement (86.8 F1 test)

method.summary: Crowdworkers on Mechanical Turk wrote questions with span answers on sampled Wikipedia paragraphs; dev and test got at least 2 extra answers. A feature-rich logistic regression, a sliding window baseline and random guess are scored with EM and F1 against humans.

datasets.name: SQuAD v1.0
datasets.split: 80% train / 10% dev / 10% test split by article
datasets.source: Top 10000 English Wikipedia articles by Project Nayuki PageRank, 536 sampled uniformly; freely available at stanford-qa.com
datasets.preprocessing: Images, figures, tables stripped; paragraphs under 500 characters discarded

models.name: Logistic regression
models.architecture: log-linear model over candidate constituents with lexicalized and dependency path features
models.context: the sentence containing the candidate answer

models.name: Sliding window (+ distance extension)
models.architecture: unigram/bigram overlap then Richardson et al. 2013 sliding window; sentence used as context

training.objective: multiclass log-likelihood loss over candidate spans (constituents); non-constituent answers replaced by the shortest containing constituent
training.batch_size: all questions in a paragraph per update
training.epochs: three passes over the training data
training.regularisation: L2, coefficient 0.1 divided by the number of batches

other.note: increasing L2 further hurt dev performance

inference.decoding: highest-scoring candidate constituent in the sentence

other.candidate_generation: constituents from Stanford CoreNLP parse rather than all O(L^2) spans

metrics.name: Exact match
metrics.definition: percentage of predictions matching any one ground truth answer exactly, ignoring punctuation and articles

metrics.name: F1
metrics.definition: bag-of-token F1, maximum over ground truth answers per question, averaged over questions; ignores punctuation and articles

eval.protocol: Single run reported on dev and test v1.0; no seeds or significance test; humans scored with second answer as prediction.

evidence.quote: Workers were asked to spend 4 minutes on every paragraph, and paid $9 per hour

results.claim: Humans score 77.0 EM and 86.8 F1 on the test set when the second answer is scored against the others.
results.setup: SQuAD v1.0 test; second answer is the prediction, remaining >=2 answers are references
results.quote: The resulting human performance score on the test set is 77.0% for the exact match metric, and 86.8% for F1.

results.claim: Logistic regression reaches 51.0 F1 on dev and test.
results.setup: SQuAD v1.0 test; candidates restricted to constituents; 180M features
results.table: Table 5, row Logistic Regression, column F1 Test

results.claim: Logistic regression exact match is 40.4 on test (40.0 dev).
results.table: Table 5, row Logistic Regression, column Exact Match Test

results.claim: Human dev F1 is 90.5 and EM 80.3, higher than on test.
results.setup: SQuAD v1.0 dev, same human protocol
results.note: Test human F1 is 86.8; dev vs test human scores differ
results.table: Table 5, row Human, column F1 Dev

results.claim: Dataset size is 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles.
results.quote: SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles

results.claim: Passage curation gives 23,215 paragraphs from 536 articles, split 80/10/10 train/dev/test.
results.setup: Top 10000 Wikipedia articles by PageRank, 536 sampled uniformly; paragraphs under 500 characters dropped
results.quote: The result was 23,215 paragraphs for the 536 articles

results.claim: 2.6% of dev and test questions were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
results.setup: Dev and test sets, second-pass workers
results.quote: 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.

results.claim: Only 77.3% of correct dev answers are constituents, an effective ceiling for the candidate-span methods.
results.setup: Dev set, ignoring punctuation and articles, Stanford CoreNLP parse
results.quote: we ﬁnd that 77.3% of the correct answers in the development set are constituents

results.claim: Logistic regression picks the sentence containing the answer 79.3% of the time.
results.note: Paper does not say whether dev or test
results.quote: the model is able to select the sentence containing the answer correctly with 79.3% accuracy

results.claim: Logistic regression dev F1 by answer type ranges from 72.1 (Date) to 31.2 (Verb Phrase) while human dev F1 is 82.4 to 95.4.
results.setup: SQuAD v1.0 dev, answer types of Table 2
results.table: Table 7, row Date, column Logistic Regression Dev F1; row Verb Phrase 31.2; Human 82.4 to 95.4

results.claim: Removing lexicalized and dependency-path features together drops dev F1 from 51.0 to 35.8; train F1 is 91.7 with all features.
results.table: Table 6, row - Lex., - Dep. Paths, column Dev

results.claim: Wang and Jiang (2016) reached 70.3 F1 on SQuAD v1.1 shortly after release.
results.setup: SQuAD v1.1, results on v1.0 said to be similar
results.quote: Wang and Jiang (2016) obtained 70.3% F1 on SQuAD v1.1

results.claim: Answer types: dates and other numbers 19.8%, proper nouns 32.6%, common noun phrases 31.8%, others 15.8%.
results.setup: Dev set, automatic categorisation with CoreNLP

results.claim: 64.1% of 192 manually labelled dev questions show syntactic variation; 33.3% synonymy; 13.6% multiple-sentence reasoning; 6.1% ambiguous.
results.setup: 192 dev questions (4 from each of 48 articles), categories overlap
results.table: Table 3, row Syntactic variation, column Percentage

results.claim: Metric definitions: EM matches any one ground truth exactly; F1 is bag-of-token F1, maximised over references then averaged; both ignore punctuation and articles.
results.note: No other normalisation (lowercasing, whitespace) is described
results.quote: We take the maximum F1 over all of the ground truth answers for a given question, and then average over all of the questions.

limits: Answers are spans, more constrained than interpretative questions (Introduction).
Only 77.3% of answers are constituents, capping the baselines.
Human score is inter-annotator agreement, differing by non-essential words; dev 90.5 vs test 86.8 F1.
Questions always have an answer in the passage; 2.6% marked unanswerable by at least one worker but no unanswerable questions are included.
All results on v1.0; later models and v1.1 not covered.

terms.definition: minimum edit distance (deletions or insertions) between unlexicalized dependency paths from an anchor to the wh-word and to the answer span, over all anchors
